title: Himalayan mountainside moved 40cm before avalanche killed 1,451 in Nepal, scientists reveal - The European Magazine
description: Himalayan mountainside moved 40cm before avalanche killed 1,451 in Nepal, scientists reveal  The European Magazine
publisher.title: The European Magazine
full_article:
Satellite images reveal possible warning signs weeks before 132 million cubic metres of rock and ice crashed into a Himalayan valley, unleashing a catastrophic flood that left thousands missing. The European’s Editor-at-Large Stanley Johnson has visited the disaster zone as scientists investigate whether global warming contributed to the collapse





A Himalayan mountainside moved by as much as 40 centimetres in the weeks before a catastrophic avalanche that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal, according to a new scientific investigation into the disaster.

Satellite observations revealed signs of instability before an estimated 132 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice broke away from the Langtang Lirung massif on 26 August, sending a devastating torrent of mud, water and debris through communities along the Nepal–China border.

The collapse left at least 1,451 people dead and another 5,745 missing in Nepal, according to figures published by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) this month. Chinese authorities reported a further 43 deaths and 519 people missing.

Scientists have yet to establish the exact cause, but believe weaknesses in the rock, changes to glaciers and possibly rising temperatures may have played a part.

The report also suggests that an earthquake, initially suspected as a possible cause, was unlikely to have triggered the avalanche.

The findings are contained in a 36-page report by ICIMOD, which examines satellite observations, seismic records, drone imagery and field investigations to establish what happened, why the mountainside failed and whether similar disasters could be anticipated.





An excavator works among buildings buried beneath tonnes of rock, mud and debris following the catastrophic Himalayan avalanche. The disaster swept through communities along the Nepal–China border, leaving widespread destruction and thousands of people dead or missing. Credit: Jitendra Raj Bajracharya/ICIMOD



The European’s Editor-at-Large, Stanley Johnson, visited the affected area on 5 October with ICIMOD researchers Pradeep Man Dangol and Prasana Dangol, as part of a visit to Nepal at the invitation of the organisation’s director-general, DrPema Gyamtsho.

Johnson, who also visited Tibet while researching his forthcoming book The Third Pole , said the devastation was almost impossible to comprehend.

He said: “The sheer scale of the devastation is almost impossible to comprehend. An entire section of a Himalayan mountain simply gave way, unleashing an enormous mass of rock and ice that swept through the valley below.

“Standing there and seeing the aftermath for myself, I was struck by the terrifying force of what had happened and the dreadful human cost. It is a sobering reminder of just how vulnerable communities living in the shadow of these great mountains can be.”

According to the ICIMOD investigation, the collapse began at approximately 8.37am local time on 26 August, when a vast section of bedrock broke away from the northern side of Langtang Lirung at an altitude of around 5,200 metres, taking part of a glacier with it.

The enormous mass plunged almost vertically for approximately 1,200 metres into the Lhende Khola Valley, breaking apart and transforming into a fast-moving torrent of rock, sediment, ice and water.





Homes stand partially buried in thick deposits of mud, rock and sediment after the avalanche sent a devastating torrent through the Himalayan river valley. The force of the disaster damaged buildings and infrastructure across the border region. Credit: Jitendra Raj Bajracharya/ICIMOD



Scientists estimate that the collapse involved 115 million cubic metres of rock and 17 million cubic metres of glacial ice, although the figures require further verification.

The material swept through the Gyirong–Rasuwagadhi border corridor, travelling down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems and destroying buildings, infrastructure and sections of the river valley.

Satellite observations have since revealed that the mountainside may have been showing signs of instability for several weeks before the disaster.

Researchers examining images taken between 7 July and 24 August identified apparent movement of up to 40 centimetres in the area that subsequently collapsed. A separate analysis covering 26 July to 19 August recorded displacement of up to 30 centimetres.

The measurements suggest that the rock-and-ice system may have been gradually deforming, although researchers say further investigation is needed to determine precisely what they represent and whether similar observations could provide reliable warnings of future collapses.





The view through a shattered building reveals the scale of the destruction, with exposed reinforcement bars, collapsed concrete and thick deposits of sediment left behind by the flood. Scientists estimate that the original mountainside collapse released approximately 132 million cubic metres of rock and ice. Credit: Jitendra Raj Bajracharya/ICIMOD



Scientists have also examined seismic records to establish whether an earthquake triggered the avalanche, as initially suspected.

The collapse generated seismic waves detected around the world, with instruments recording signals equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake.

Analysis indicates that the major seismic disturbance was caused by the mountainside itself falling, making an earthquake an unlikely immediate trigger.

With the sequence of events established, the investigation has focused on why such an enormous section of rock and ice became unstable.

One possible explanation involves geological weaknesses that may have existed for years. Satellite images taken in December 2017 and January 2026 showed features in the mountainside that scientists believe could represent long-standing fractures in the rock.

Researchers have also considered whether the devastating 2015 Nepal earthquake weakened the mountain. The earthquake caused a catastrophic failure on another side of Langtang Lirung, burying Langtang village, although any connection with the August 2026 collapse remains unproven.

Changes to the glacier attached to the mountainside may also have contributed. Evidence suggests that its thickness had altered over previous years, potentially adding weight to an already unstable rock face.

The report additionally examines the possible effects of accumulated snow and ice and repeated freezing and thawing, which can weaken fractured rock over time.

Scientists are particularly interested in whether rising temperatures contributed to these processes, amid growing concern about the effects of global warming throughout the Hindu Kush Himalayan region.

ICIMOD reports that the rate of glacier mass loss across the region has nearly doubled since 2000, with the 2024–25 monitoring year recording the greatest losses in the series examined.

As glaciers retreat, they can expose mountainsides previously supported by ice, leaving fractured rock more vulnerable to instability. Changes in the weight and thickness of glaciers can also alter the forces acting on surrounding slopes.

Rising temperatures can contribute to another potential source of instability – the degradation of permafrost, or ground that ordinarily remains frozen and can help hold fractured rock together.

Researchers found that the disaster area lay within a zone where permafrost may have existed, although they could not establish whether thawing had occurred at the precise location of the collapse.





Two residents survey the damage to their community, where buildings have been left surrounded by rubble and sediment. The disaster has raised urgent questions about the vulnerability of settlements along Himalayan rivers and the effectiveness of existing early-warning systems. Credit: Jitendra Raj Bajracharya/ICIMOD



Unusually warm conditions in 2026 are also being examined as scientists investigate whether higher temperatures, changes to glacier ice and weakening permafrost may have combined with existing geological fractures to destabilise the mountainside.

However, the report explicitly states that there is no direct evidence linking rapid glacier melting to the August disaster. Scientists have not established whether global warming contributed to the collapse or identified any single factor as its dominant cause.

The catastrophe caused extensive damage to Nepal’s infrastructure, destroying or damaging 13 operational and under-construction hydropower projects, affecting infrastructure equivalent to approximately one-tenth of the country’s installed electricity-generating capacity.

Hydropower accounted for approximately 44 per cent of the physical damage assessed across the affected sectors, with losses estimated at nearly 120 billion Nepalese rupees.

The flood also devastated the Gyirong border port, where a powerful wave of debris travelled approximately three kilometres upstream. Two temporary lakes formed following the collapse and subsequently drained without causing another major disaster.

The speed of the avalanche left communities closest to the mountainside with little opportunity to escape. The debris surge reached the border corridor within approximately seven minutes of the initial collapse.

Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology reportedly sent text-message alerts to approximately 679,000 people in downstream districts at around 9.15am, after the first communities along the border corridor had already been struck.

The disaster has exposed limitations in existing warning systems, which are designed primarily to detect heavy rainfall and rising river levels rather than sudden rock-and-ice avalanches high in the mountains.

The Gyirong–Rasuwagadhi corridor had already suffered a major flood in July 2025 when a lake on Tibet’s Purepu Glacier suddenly released its water, destroying the Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China.

Scientists are also examining another recent rock-and-ice avalanche in Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki basin, where satellite imagery has confirmed a separate mountain collapse and glacier failure.

The two latest disasters, occurring within seven weeks of each other, have intensified concern about the dangers facing Himalayan communities and the difficulties of identifying unstable mountainsides before catastrophic failures occur.

ICIMOD has called for improved satellite monitoring of vulnerable slopes, better seismic detection, coordinated early-warning arrangements and faster communication between countries sharing mountain river systems.

Researchers believe identifying dangerous mountainsides before they collapse could help authorities assess risks and improve emergency preparations, even where scientists cannot predict precisely when a failure will occur.





A pair of trees stands among ruined buildings and thick deposits of rock and mud in the aftermath of the disaster. The enormous volume of material carried downstream transformed sections of the river valley, leaving homes buried and entire areas almost unrecognisable. Credit: Jitendra Raj Bajracharya/ICIMOD



During his visit to Nepal, Johnson also spoke to David Silsen, the World Bank’s Country Director for Nepal, who warned that the consequences of warming in the Himalayan region could extend far beyond the countries immediately affected.

“The effect of global warming in the Hindu-Kush Himalayan region may be as important to the world’s future as the destruction of the Amazon rainforest,” Silsen told Johnson.

The Hindu Kush Himalaya supplies water to major Asian river networks, making the condition of its glaciers, snow cover and mountain environments important to millions of people throughout the continent.

Johnson said the scientific investigation could have profound implications for the future of the region if a connection between the disaster and rising temperatures is established.

“If scientists establish that global warming played a part in this disaster, the implications could be deeply troubling,” he said.

“It would raise serious questions about what the future holds for the Himalayas and the millions of people who depend on them.

“We must be careful not to jump to conclusions about the cause, but if rising temperatures are making these mountains more unstable, it would underline just how urgently the world needs to tackle climate change.”

ICIMOD works across eight countries – Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan – to research environmental change and strengthen regional cooperation.

Dr Pema Gyamtsho, its director general, said: “The speed and force of the flood, carrying large volumes of water, sediment, and boulders through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, are deeply concerning.

“The potential for impacts further downstream is a reminder of how quickly a hazard in the mountains can become a wider regional concern. It also reinforces the importance of timely information, early warnings, preparedness, and coordinated action.”

He added: “On behalf of ICIMOD, I extend our solidarity to the people and the Governments of Nepal and China at this difficult time. We stand ready to support the ongoing response and recovery efforts, drawing on the knowledge, science, data, and expertise available to us.

“My heart also goes out to the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives and to all those enduring the consequences of this tragedy.”







READ MORE: New Hindu Kush Himalaya glacier reports warn of deepening risk to Asia’s water security. New reports published today lay bare the accelerating loss of ice across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, where glaciers are retreating at increasing speed in a region critical to the water security of nearly two billion people. Here, our editor-at-large Stanley Johnson, drawing on his long career as an environmentalist and ahead of the 30 March re-release of his book In the Footsteps of Marco Polo, reflects on changes to a mountain system whose fate matters far beyond the high Pamirs.

title: Nepal’s disaster is an urgent wake-up call - Nature
description: Nepal’s disaster is an urgent wake-up call  Nature
publisher.title: Nature
full_article:
On 26 August, an avalanche and massive flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district. Thousands of lives were lost, homes were destroyed, roads and energy infrastructure were washed away, and trade and tourism were disrupted.

Disaster early-warning systems can succeed — but collective action is needed

This catastrophe should not be treated as just another disaster. It is the latest — and worst — in a series of exceptionally massive deluges of rock, ice and debris from mountains. The unprecedented scale of the damage shows that current approaches of assessing and managing these risks have failed. Moreover, with global warming accelerating, further disasters of this magnitude are expected.

How scientists analyse and officials manage environmental risks in mountainous regions must urgently be restructured. Here we outline how such hazards are changing and propose how researchers can assess coupled, cascading risks to protect communities and save lives.

Successive extreme disasters

The Rasuwa disaster is not a freak event. Over the past few years, the world has seen several similar massive rock and ice collapses with ensuing floods (see ‘Cascading risks’).

Sources: M. C. Matthew et al. Landslides 21, 2307–2326 (2024); D. Schneider et al. Earth Surf. Process. Landf. 36, 1948–1966 (2011); Y. Zhong et al. Landslides 22, 989–1001 (2025); J. A. Coe et al. Landslides 15, 393–407 (2018); A. Kääb et al. Cryosphere 15, 1751–1785 (2021); Alaska Volcano Observatory yearly reports (https://avo.alaska.edu)

In February 2021 in India, an avalanche from Ronti peak led to a huge flood in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand. The flow of water and debris devastated the Ronti Gad valley, killing more than 200 people and destroying hydropower structures1.

Just a few months later, in June 2021 in Nepal, a small glacial lake burst its banks, sending flood waters surging into the Melamchi River. This triggered a cascade of hazards that washed away more than 50 million cubic metres of sediment and altered river-bed levels by roughly 20 metres in some places2. Around 600 people were displaced and at least 20 died. The region’s freshly established drinking-water infrastructure was severely damaged and vast areas of agricultural land were lost.

Losing your way of life to climate change matters — and we need a way to measure it

Similarly, in October 2023 in Sikkim, India, a massive slide of glacial sediment into South Lhonak glacier lake initiated another outburst and flood. The waters swept an incredible 270 million m3 of sediment down the Teesta River. More than 100 people died, around 26,000 buildings were damaged and hydropower structures were destroyed. The impacts, including infrastructure damage, affected Bangladesh, too3.

Furthermore, in May 2025, the village of Blatten in the Swiss Alps was buried under an avalanche that released nearly 10 million m3 of rock and ice after a glacier collapsed. The glacier was weakened by a series of rock slides that deposited material onto it4. The village was destroyed and there was one fatality, but the other residents were evacuated before it was inundated.

And, in Alaska, less than three months later, an extraordinary landslide (roughly 64 million m3) crashed onto South Sawyer Glacier and into Tracy Arm Fjord5, generating a tsunami with heights of close to 500 m. Fortunately, this happened a few hours before cruise ships would have been travelling through the fjord, avoiding what might have been a maritime disaster.

Roads, bridges and other infrastructure were swept away by the water after the August avalanche in Nepal. Credit: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto via Getty

The Rasuwa disaster exceeds these events. On the northern slopes of Langtang Lirung mountain, a failure in the bedrock caused a massive rock avalanche that took the overlying glacier with it. The resulting avalanche (around 125 million m3 of rock and ice) is one of the largest on record worldwide.

As the ice, debris and water rushed down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river valleys, the ice melted and extra sediment and water were incorporated into the flow. Damage extended over 100 kilometres from the source. More than 1,400 people have died, more than 5,000 are missing and tens of thousands have been displaced. Settlements, roads and bridges were washed away and around 10% of Nepal’s hydropower production was knocked out. Reconstruction costs have been put at around US$5 billion.

And on 11 October, the Himalaya region of central Nepal was hit by floods in the upper Budhi Gandaki river valley that were triggered by another large rock and ice avalanche from a steep mountain slope. The avalanche was around half the size of the August collapse. The floods damaged settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower structures.

Growing hazards and exposure

These events resulted from a combination of interacting and cascading processes: collapses of steep rock or glacier slopes, failures of banks of sediment, outburst floods from lakes and further entrainment of water, debris and sediment by the flood as it raced downstream.

The scientific community knows this and has repeatedly signalled the need for an improved understanding of these cascading hazards and for them to be incorporated into risk analyses6,7. But, so far, little has changed in how such hazards and risks are considered in practice.

The likelihood of one-off events is typically gauged on the basis of the historical record. But events at the scale that we are now seeing are rare or missing from those archives. That makes it hard to predict how frequently massive avalanche-triggered floods might occur in future — the number seen over the past few years is too small to determine long-term trends. But one thing is certain: the world is warming, meaning further rock-slope failures and glacier collapses are likely to occur in coming decades. What has happened historically will not be a good model for what is to come.

Expanding development in mountainous areas is also increasing the exposure of people, settlements and infrastructure to hazards. For example, hydropower development in the Trishuli basin in Rasuwa has expanded since 2010, as has development along the road to the Rasuwagadhi–Kerung border between China and Nepal.

Re-evaluate risk analysis

Scientists and decision makers must rethink how they analyse hazards and risks in mountainous regions. Rather than a single method, we propose a complementary set of approaches that can be combined as needed depending on the context.

First, define the purpose and scope of the assessment. For instance, a risk analysis can inform land-use planning, guide funding allocations, identify protection gaps, calculate potential economic losses or establish priorities for risk management at scales ranging from a single hydropower plant to large populated areas. Together, governments and local communities need to decide what level of risk they are willing to tolerate and consider how to protect the most-vulnerable groups and infrastructure.

Second, we suggest applying a combination of several risk-evaluation methodologies. Each approach covers a specific risk aspect and is complemented by the others. Disasters such as the one in Rasuwa underline the importance of using several tools to capture the multifaceted impacts comprehensively.

Probabilistic risk analysis can be used to compute the distribution of asset losses for events of various sizes and frequencies8. For example, for a hydropower plant, such an analysis might provide a statistical representation of the extent of damage in relation to different event probabilities.

AI to the rescue: how to enhance disaster early warnings with tech tools

However, performing a probabilistic analysis is challenging when assessing future events that have few or no precedents. In such cases, we suggest that analysts consider using models of credible, physically plausible scenarios. These can be built from likelihoods and judgements based on existing knowledge9 and by extending the analysis to a wide range of possible events.

For this, the geological record can sometimes provide clues. For example, in Rasuwa, large boulders lying well beyond the current river bed are testimonies of similar floods some 5,000 years ago10. A plausibility analysis would then check whether such an event is plausible under current or near-future conditions.

Storyline approaches that consider a range of far-reaching possibilities in both qualitative and quantitative ways should be applied to explore cascading effects beyond current populations and structures11. For instance, the Rasuwa disaster destroyed important trade and transport routes between Nepal and China with consequences for Nepal’s economy. The destruction of hydropower sites also affects neighbouring countries that depend on energy imports, including Bangladesh.

Risk-network analysis can be used to address gaps in risk assessments, such as the lack of inclusion of the consequences for disadvantaged populations. Such methods evaluate, for example, connections between flooded houses and their inhabitants, lost local businesses and livelihoods, and disruptions to social networks and education and health-care services.

title: Nepal Premier League to introduce DRS for third edition - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal Premier League to introduce DRS for third edition  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Nepal Premier League will introduce the Decision Review System (DRS) in its third edition, scheduled to run from October 26 to November 21.

The Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) announced the move on social media on Tuesday, paving the way for teams to challenge on-field umpiring decisions during the tournament.

CAN Secretary Paras Khadka had earlier said preparations were underway to bring DRS to the league. According to Khadka, two companies had already tested the technology, with a final decision to be made after assessing its accuracy and reliability.

CAN said the system would use full 3D ball-tracking technology to review leg-before-wicket (LBW) decisions. Reviews would also be available for run-outs, stumpings and no-ball calls.

The system will also use artificial intelligence-based edge detection to determine whether the ball has touched the bat, helping umpires assess potential edges.

title: Seven Alpine-Style Climbs Happening Now in Nepal - Explorersweb »
description: Seven Alpine-Style Climbs Happening Now in Nepal  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
Several small teams are attempting difficult climbs on Nepal’s 6,000 and 7,000m peaks. Unfortunately, they rarely report on their plans or progress until they return, and often only if they succeed.

This is what we know about the ongoing expeditions:

Three young French climbers, members of the Military High Mountain Group from Chamonix, celebrated their organization’s 50th anniversary with a new route on Peak 41. This 6,654m mountain is located in the Khumbu region and is often called the “true Mera Peak.”

Konrad Piontek, Amaury Fouillade, and Clovis Paulin took advantage of a good weather window and achieved the first ascent of the peak’s northeast face. They climbed in an alpine-style single push over four days. The result is a beautiful 1,400m line with difficulties up to ED+ 5+ M6 A1 90°. They descended via the southeast face. The team named their line Bon Matin (good morning).

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Jugal II

Nivel Meroi and Romano Benet are acclimatized and ready to attempt a new route on Jugal II, but the Italian couple will be on their own. Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, has left due to illness.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Jannu

Meanwhile, in the Kangchenjunga region, a large Russian team has also finished acclimatizing. The team trekked in the area and crossed a number of high-altitude passes, the latest of them at the top of an icefall at 5,750m. They reported lots of snow above 5,000m but are ready to attempt a new route on the formidable Jannu (7,710m) from its southeast side.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

The team comprises Ivan Artemov, Ivan Volkov, Artem Zhdanov, Konstantin Neumoin, Roman Shilin, and Vasily Yagodin.

Gangapurna West

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan traveled to Nepal in September, aiming to achieve the first ascent of Gangapurna West (7,455m), also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal. They have provided no news since, but they probably had to retreat when an intense snowstorm hit the Annapurna region three weeks ago.

Location of Gangapurna West on a Google Earth screenshot. Notes by Lindsay Griffin for the American Alpine Journal.

Meanwhile, a second team has reached the base of the peak with the same objective. Valery Shamalo, Natalia Zanina, Maksim Trufanov, and Ruslan Kirichenko arrived at the beginning of October and saw no one else there. They reported that recent precipitation had left the trail in a poor state; the climbers had to cross landslides and swollen rivers to reach base camp.

The team has completed two acclimatization climbs, looking for a passage through the icefall at the base of the mountain and then a series of couloirs. They reached 5,900m and, on a second trip, 6,600m. Deep snow covered the peak, which slowed progress. Finally, they launched a summit bid last week.

From 6,600m, they spent a day on technical ice sections of 70–80º. In poor visibility, they endured spindrift and were showered by small ice chunks.

“In the afternoon, the weather deteriorated sharply,” Natalia Zanina said. “Heavy snowfall began, and we started being struck by large, continuous avalanches. At 6,800m (340m from the summit), we decided to turn back.”

https://explorersweb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/video-gangapurna.mp4

A note on names: according to 8000ers.com , Asapurna should be the correct name for this peak because — although it is closer to Gangapurna — Asapurna’s summit ridge connects directly to Annapurna III.

Mystery teams

The list of climbing permits granted by Nepal’s Ministry of Tourism points to some other interesting expeditions, some of them in remote western Nepal. There is a permit for Nyalu Kang (6,265m), only opened to foreign climbers in 2024 and reportedly unclimbed, and Ardang, summited once by Canadians Bryce Kendall and Sunny Twelker in 2019. Victor Saunders and Mick Fowler of the UK attempted Ardang last year.

full_article:
The Nepal Automobiles’ Association (NASA Nepal) has recently organised the Nepal Sim Racing National Championship 2026 at the International Sports Complex, Lalitpur, Nepal. Supported by the FIA Motorsport Funding Programme, the project has strengthened grassroots motor sport development in Nepal by providing sim racing training to over 400 young people.

The Championship comprised of four regional competitions and one national championship and offered regional exposure to the junior and senior winners who demonstrated promising talent on the two FIA-accredited sim racing simulators NASA Nepal has purchased to enable the competition.

In the Senior category, Jay Pratap Maskey finished first, followed by Niman Shakya. Maskey recorded a best lap time of approximately 1 minute 22 seconds on the Circuit de Lédenon. In the Junior category, Kushal Bhandari secured first place, followed by Sparsha Byanju and Binit Maharjan. The Promotional Challenge category was won by Bhushan Kumar Shrestha. Winners received cash prizes, medals and certificates.

The championship was conducted using advanced sim racing technology and the iRacing platform, allowing participants to compete on internationally recognised virtual circuits. The event provided an opportunity to develop racing skills, precision, strategic thinking and competitive discipline in a structured digital motor sport environment.

The championship was officially opened by NASA Nepal President Dasarath Risal and Chandra Kumar Rai, Chief of the International Sports Complex, Satdobato. Through the Esport Championship in Nepal project, NASA Nepal aims to expand access to motor sport, identify emerging talent and create new opportunities for young people to participate in the sport, contributing to the continued development of motor sport in Nepal in line with the FIA’s commitment to doubling global participation.

title: Nepal Isn’t Asking for Charity. It’s Calling in a Debt. - Progressive.org
description: Nepal Isn’t Asking for Charity. It’s Calling in a Debt.  Progressive.org
publisher.title: Progressive.org
full_article:
When a piece of Himalayan glacier broke loose above the Bhotekoshi River in August, it sent a wall of water, ice, and rock hurtling at alarming speeds through Nepal’s northern districts in mere minutes. More than 1,400 people are now confirmed dead, and more than 4,000 remain unaccounted for. Entire villages were destroyed. Nepal’s government estimates damage at $2.7 billion and reconstruction at $4.7 billion, a staggering sum for a country whose entire budget averages $14 billion annually.

Nepal did little to nothing to cause the warming, melting, and extreme precipitation plaguing its glaciers. In the weeks after the disaster, Nepal’s government filed a formal claim to the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FLRD), a financial mechanism operated by the United Nations. The claim demands wealthy countries make good on a climate promise they made in 2022 to finance the recovery of vulnerable communities from climate-related damage. The country hasn’t had luck yet, but advocates hope the upcoming U.N. climate conference—the thirty-first annual Conference of the Parties, or COP31—will pressure the fund’s board to uphold the agreement.

The FRLD was created in 2023 at the COP27 climate negotiations to fund climate-driven disaster recovery initiatives in the wake of the devastating 2022 floods in Pakistan, which killed or injured 15,000, displaced nearly eight million people, and destroyed or damaged millions of homes and acres of agricultural land. But its creation took decades. Demands for compensation for climate-caused losses and damages by developing countries date back to the United Nations’s earliest climate talks, including a 1991 proposal for such a fund by the South Pacific archipelago nation of Vanuatu and the Alliance of Small Island States.

The fund, whose board is hosted by the Philippines and its secretariat run by the World Bank, operates as a grant- and project-based financing mechanism. Climate-vulnerable developing countries can apply for access to the fund’s resources, which come primarily from governments, but also allow private sector partnerships and innovative financing mechanisms.

Three years into its existence, the FRLD has yet to approve a single funding request tied to a specific disaster. Faced with its first real test, the fund, built to respond to climate-fueled disasters, showed it is unprepared to respond quickly. That’s in part because only about a third of the roughly $822 million pledged by developed countries to the fund since 2023 has actually been transferred. The fund’s own rules cap initial disbursements at $20 million per project—roughly half a percent of Nepal’s low-end damage estimate—regardless of how fast the board moves.

At the end of August, Nepali officials wrote to the board of the FRLD requesting financial support in the wake of the catastrophic floods, invoking the very language of climate justice the fund was built to honor. But the FRLD’s current funding window closed in June.

“We are genuinely suffering from the adverse effects of climate change,” states the letter, which was obtained by The Kathmandu Post . “Time is of the essence. A prompt response would help protect affected populations, restore essential services, prevent further suffering and demonstrate that the fund can translate international solidarity into timely support for vulnerable countries and communities when it is most urgently needed.”

The Nepali government argues that a country that has contributed so little to global climate emissions should not have to bear the scale and cost of what is equivalent to a “Himalayan tsunami” alone. “Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible,” Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said in an interview with The Kathmandu Post . “Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create. The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change.”

Before the floods in August, Nepal was already reportedly poised to receive $20 million from the fund for an application filed for unrelated energy, health, and food-security projects under the fund’s previous grant window. More than 100 countries are in line behind Nepal.

On September 9, the FRLD’s co-chairs wrote back to Kathmandu with “deepest sympathies” and “unwavering solidarity,” pledging to work with the board to address the request “as rapidly as possible.” Their promise, though, does not commit to any specifics in terms of timing or dollar amounts.

More than a dozen board members from Asia, Africa, Latin America, and small island states pushed for an emergency session to vote on Nepal’s requests. In a letter addressed to the board, its co-chairs, and executive director, they wrote, “This event constitutes precisely the kind of climate-related extreme weather events the Fund was established to address . . . . The scale of loss of life, displacement, and destruction of energy, transport, and economic infrastructure warrants the Board’s urgent consideration of how the Fund’s existing instruments should be mobilized to support Nepal’s government and affected communities.”

On October 18, the board’s co-chairs announced a special meeting for October 22.

One board member, South African negotiator Richard Sherman, has suggested the board could realistically designate another $20 million for Nepal’s current claim during the emergency meeting, while noting that it would be largely symbolic against the scale of the damage.

Nepal’s request came just two months before COP31 opens in Antalya, Turkiye, where United Nations climate negotiators will meet to continue hammering out the best ways to implement and fund the commitments of the Paris Agreement. For years, debates, particularly around climate-related damages, have been largely speculative—delegates have fought over projections and estimations.

Nepal has turned that speculative exercise into a real test: How does a fund respond to a sudden onset disaster, the very climate impacts it was intended to address, when it has no fast-track funding authority?

No amount of money can erase what Nepal has lost, or what will take years to rebuild. Nepali communities are not helplessly waiting in the wings expecting aid to fall from the sky. They have crowdfunded nearly $90 million for response, making the case that this disaster was climate-driven. They have built a technical case that strikes at the core of the fund’s modus operandi .

If the loss and damage fund cannot move for Nepal—which has endured more than 1,400 deaths and thousands more missing, and has a formal claim on the table and a board that acknowledges the need to consider its urgent request—it is hard to imagine the scenario in which it moves for anyone. Nepal has done its part. The fund and the governments who built it must now do theirs.

In its appeal to the FRLD board, Nepal’s government directly asked the board to act before its next meeting in December, noting that time was of the essence. Whether the fund and its donors will honor this claim is now an open question with consequences that extend far beyond Nepal.

full_article:
A single-centre retrospective observational study in Nepal found that patients with ALK- or ROS1-positive non-small cell lung cancer commonly had a history of non-smoking and were diagnosed with advanced-stage disease. The abstract reports that the analysis included 51 immunohistochemistry-positive cases with complete clinical data: 42 ALK-positive cases and nine ROS1-positive cases. Two of the ALK-positive cases were inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors rather than non-small cell lung cancers, leaving 49 lung cancers in the selected cohort.

The tertiary-care study initially covered 6,078 cancer cases, including 670 lung cancers and 560 cases of non-small cell lung cancer. All 560 non-small cell lung cancer cases underwent immunohistochemistry-based screening for ALK and ROS1. Among the 51 selected positive cases, the median age was 53 years, with a range of 26–82 years, and 53% were male. Eighty percent were non-smokers, 71% had stage IV disease, and adenocarcinoma was the predominant histological subtype, accounting for 65% of cases. Exploratory comparisons between the ALK and ROS1 subgroups showed no statistically significant differences in the evaluated clinicopathological characteristics.

All 51 patients had documented initiation of first-line crizotinib. The median time from diagnosis to tyrosine kinase inhibitor initiation was 0.82 months, with an interquartile range of 1.25 months, and the median observed duration of first-line treatment was 17.9 months, with an interquartile range of 22.6 months. Twelve patients, representing 23.5% of the cohort, subsequently received lorlatinib. Based on available clinical follow-up, the estimated median time to first-line treatment discontinuation was 36.4 months, with a 95% confidence interval of 27.0 months to not reached. Median progression-free survival was 41.7 months, with the same confidence interval, while median overall survival was not reached.

The Nepal Automobiles' Association (NASA Nepal) recently organized the Nepal Sim Racing National Championship 2026 at the International Sports Complex in Lalitpur, Nepal. Supported by the FIA Motorsport Funding Program, the project has strengthened grassroots motorsports development in Nepal by providing sim racing training to more than 400 young people.

The championship comprised four regional competitions and one national championship, offering regional exposure to the junior and senior winners, who demonstrated promising talent on the two FIA-accredited sim racing simulators NASA Nepal purchased to support the competition.

The championship used advanced sim racing technology and the iRacing platform, allowing participants to compete on internationally recognized virtual circuits. The event provided an opportunity to develop racing skills, precision, strategic thinking and competitive discipline in a structured digital motorsports environment.

The championship was officially opened by NASA Nepal President Dasarath Risal and Chandra Kumar Rai, chief of the International Sports Complex in Satdobato.

Through the Esport Championship in Nepal project, NASA Nepal aims to expand access to motorsports, identify emerging talent, and create new opportunities for young people to participate in the sport. The initiative supports the continued development of motorsports in Nepal in line with the FIA's commitment to doubling global participation.

In the senior category, Jay Pratap Maskey finished first, followed by Niman Shakya. Maskey recorded a best lap time of approximately 1 minute 22 seconds on the Circuit de Lédenon. In the junior category, Kushal Bhandari secured first place, followed by Sparsha Byanju and Binit Maharjan. Bhushan Kumar Shrestha won the Promotional Challenge category. Winners received cash prizes, medals and certificates.

title: Survey-weighted cross-sectional study links Nepal insurance enrollment with higher curative healthcare use - Bioengineer.org
description: Survey-weighted cross-sectional study links Nepal insurance enrollment with higher curative healthcare use  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
A survey-weighted cross-sectional study in Suryabinayak municipality, Nepal, found that households enrolled in the National Health Insurance Program reported more use of several healthcare services than uninsured households, while preventive service use showed no overall association. The available abstract reports overall utilization of 74.7% among insured households and 53.6% among uninsured households, a statistically significant difference. In adjusted analyses, enrollment was associated with higher odds of overall, outpatient, diagnostic, emergency and inpatient service use, but not preventive services overall.

Researchers conducted a community-based comparative cross-sectional survey from June to July 2025. They randomly selected five of Suryabinayak’s 10 administrative wards, then used two-stage stratified random sampling to recruit 301 households in Bhaktapur: 150 with National Health Insurance Program enrollment and 151 without it. Utilization outcomes covered overall service use, outpatient visits, diagnostic services, emergency care, inpatient admissions and preventive services during the preceding six months. The analysis used survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression, with potential confounders identified through a directed acyclic graph. The authors also assessed robustness using Firth’s penalized regression, inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting and sensitivity analyses.

After adjustment, insurance enrollment was associated with higher odds of overall healthcare utilization (adjusted odds ratio, aOR, 2.69; 95% confidence interval, 1.56–4.63). The abstract also reports associations with outpatient use (aOR 2.13), diagnostic services (aOR 2.57), emergency care (aOR 2.81) and hospital admission (aOR 2.21), and says these findings were consistent across the sensitivity analyses. Preventive service use did not differ significantly between insured and uninsured households in the unadjusted comparison (p=0.617), and enrollment was not associated with preventive use overall (aOR 1.37). That association varied by socioeconomic status: it was positive among wealthier households (aOR 3.40) but absent among poorer households (aOR 0.40).

title: Nepal’s Next Growth Story Could Be Built on Finance - Khabarhub
description: Nepal’s Next Growth Story Could Be Built on Finance  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
Nepal’s economic future is often discussed in terms of hydropower, tourism, agriculture, infrastructure and technology. Yet there is another sector that could determine whether these opportunities become engines of prosperity: finance.

Nepal’s challenge is not simply a shortage of money. It is also a shortage of effective ways to turn available financial resources into productive investment.

Every year, billions of dollars enter Nepal through remittances. Workers’ remittances have exceeded 30 percent of GDP in recent years, among the highest ratios in the world. Foreign-exchange reserves are substantial. Banks hold significant deposits, yet weak demand for productive credit has contributed to excess liquidity.

This presents an interesting paradox. There is money in the financial system, yet businesses struggle to obtain the right kind of capital. Entrepreneurs have ideas but limited access to risk finance. Infrastructure requires long-term funding. Start-ups need equity rather than conventional loans secured against property. Household savings often have relatively few productive investment choices.

The question, therefore, is not simply whether Nepal has enough finance. It is whether Nepal’s financial system is doing enough to create wealth.

Nepal has important ingredients. Its citizens generate substantial remittances. Its households save. Its banking system has accumulated considerable financial resources. Its hydropower sector is creating valuable assets. Its young entrepreneurs have ideas. And its infrastructure and investment needs are enormous.

For decades, remittances have performed an extraordinary social and economic function. They have supported families, financed education and healthcare, helped build homes and reduced poverty.

But imagine the next stage. A Nepali working abroad sends money home. Most of it should remain available to the family that earned it. But suppose that worker could voluntarily invest a small portion, safely and transparently, in a professionally managed fund financing hydropower, tourism, infrastructure or growing Nepali businesses. The same money that supports today’s household could also help build tomorrow’s economy.

This is the transformation Nepal should seek: from remittances to savings, from savings to investment, and from investment to productive enterprises, assets and jobs.

That requires moving beyond an overwhelmingly bank-centred view of finance. Banks will remain indispensable. But banks cannot, and should not, finance everything.

A young technology company may have talented people and valuable ideas but little collateral. It needs equity. A hydropower plant may generate electricity for 30 or 40 years. It needs long-term capital. A promising Nepali company seeking to expand internationally may need growth capital rather than another short-term loan.

Municipalities need ways to finance urban infrastructure. Climate-resilient projects may require guarantees and blended finance. Large investments may eventually be financed partly through infrastructure funds or project bonds.

Each requires a different financial instrument.

Nepal’s next financial reform should not simply be about more credit. It should be about more kinds of capital.

This means building deeper capital markets alongside stronger banks: corporate bonds, infrastructure funds, venture capital, private equity, pension and insurance investment, green bonds and professionally regulated investment vehicles.

Credit and equity serve different purposes. Banks are well suited to financing businesses that can repay loans. Equity investors can share the risks of building businesses whose future earnings are uncertain.

A modern economy needs both. Nepal is not starting from zero. It has a stock exchange, insurance companies, institutional investors and specialized institutions such as Nepal Infrastructure Bank (NIFRA), established to support infrastructure financing.

The challenge is to build on these foundations, developing deeper markets, stronger institutions and financial instruments capable of mobilizing capital at scale.

There is also a larger opportunity: finance itself could become an economic sector. Singapore developed into a global financial centre. Dubai created a regional financial hub. Mauritius developed specialized international financial services. India is developing GIFT City.

Nepal neither needs nor should try to copy them. Its first priority must be to become exceptionally good at financing its own development. Over time, it could develop specialized financial services built around its comparative advantages.

Why, for example, could Nepal not become a centre of expertise in Himalayan green finance, financing hydropower, climate resilience, sustainable tourism, mountain infrastructure and nature-related investment?

Nepal sits at the intersection of some of this century’s great investment challenges: clean energy, climate adaptation, resilient infrastructure and the sustainable management of natural resources.

These are not only development challenges. Properly structured, many are also investment opportunities. Hydropower provides a particularly compelling example. Electricity exports can generate revenue. But hydropower can potentially do something more: create long-term financial assets around which domestic and international capital can be mobilized.

The objective should not merely be to build projects. It should be to build bankable assets and investable markets.

That requires credible institutions, transparent regulation, reliable financial information, strong corporate governance and confidence that contracts will be respected.

Finance ultimately runs on trust. And this is where ambition must be accompanied by discipline.

Nepal’s financial system also faces vulnerabilities. Non-performing loans have risen, while weaknesses in savings and credit cooperatives have exposed depositors to serious risks. These challenges underscore the importance of strengthening financial supervision, governance, transparency and public confidence.

Financial development cannot mean easy money or weaker regulation. Quite the opposite. The more ambitious a financial system becomes, the stronger its institutions must become.

Depositors need protection. Investors need reliable information. Banks need rigorous supervision. Capital markets need transparency. Minority shareholders need protection. Financial crime must be addressed decisively.

Without trust, savings remain cautious and investment remains short-term. With trust, domestic savings can begin financing domestic ambition.

What, then, should Nepal do? Three priorities deserve particular attention.

First, develop credible long-term financing vehicles for infrastructure and productive enterprises. This means strengthening corporate bond markets, infrastructure funds and professionally managed investment institutions capable of providing patient capital.

Second, create regulated investment opportunities through which domestic and diaspora savings can participate in Nepal’s economic growth. Financial products must be transparent, affordable and appropriate to investors’ risk tolerance. Mobilizing savings should never mean exposing families to risks they cannot understand or afford.

The next chapter of financial reform should therefore be about more than expanding banking or increasing credit. It should be about building institutions and markets that transform savings into productive investment, ideas into enterprises and infrastructure into lasting economic assets.

Third, strengthen financial supervision, corporate governance and investor protection. Without these foundations, deeper financial markets could create new vulnerabilities rather than economic opportunities.

Together, these reforms could gradually change Nepal’s financial landscape.

Imagine a ten-year ambition. A deeper bond market finances infrastructure. Pension and insurance savings provide patient capital. Venture funds support young entrepreneurs. Banks increasingly assess viable businesses on their earning potential rather than primarily on collateral. Digital finance lowers transaction costs. International investors find credible projects and predictable rules.

And Nepali companies begin raising capital to expand beyond Nepal.

That would change the development conversation. For years, developing countries have asked: Where will the money for development come from? Perhaps the better question is: How do we build a financial system capable of turning the money we already have into development?

Nepal has important ingredients. Its citizens generate substantial remittances. Its households save. Its banking system has accumulated considerable financial resources. Its hydropower sector is creating valuable assets. Its young entrepreneurs have ideas. And its infrastructure and investment needs are enormous.

What Nepal needs is a financial architecture capable of connecting these pieces more effectively.

The next chapter of financial reform should therefore be about more than expanding banking or increasing credit. It should be about building institutions and markets that transform savings into productive investment, ideas into enterprises and infrastructure into lasting economic assets.

A financial system should do more than store a nation’s wealth. It should help create its future.

If Nepal can make that transition, finance will no longer simply support its growth story. It could become one of the engines driving it.

publisher.title: Asian Hospitality
full_article:
AS NEPAL CONTINUES to recover from a massive flood in August, U.S. hoteliers are gathering aid to send to the country. The AAHOA Charitable Foundation is organizing the effort to raise funds, donations and volunteers to bring to Nepal in January.

The Aug. 26 flood, triggered by a rock-and-ice avalanche into a Himalayan mountain lake, has so far killed more than 1,400 people with more than 6000 unaccounted for, according to Big News Network. It has left more than 70,000 people homeless.

“It's so sad to see that these lives are just completely washed away, and they had no idea this was happening,” said Lina Patel, director of strategic franchise initiatives for Red Roof and one of the organizers of the ACF efforts. “We took a helicopter there to do a prayer and a puja after three weeks and you cannot tell that there was a civilization there. That whole area is back to its natural state. You cannot even see a pipe or a wire sticking out or anything. Everybody is just buried hundreds of feet under that sand and rock.”

Planning the mission

Patel regularly leads expeditions and pilgrimages in the Himalayas. She is very familiar with the area where the worst of the flood hit.

“That whole valley where villages were, that was the road that connects Nepal to China, and there was a trade route along with the Pilgrims' route, and all these villages thrive based on the trade route and the pilgrims' route,” she said. “Now that route is completely washed away, I believe the government is still deciding on what to do next.”

Fellow AAHOA lifetime members Nayna Patel, Maya Patel and Manisha Patel are serving with Lina as liaisons between ACF and Child Environment Nepal to coordinate delivery of the aid. The women, all of whom have traveled with Lina to Nepal previously, will cover their own travel expenses to visit affected communities, communicate local needs and share updates on approved relief efforts, according to ACF.

Along with cash donations, ACF are collecting staple foods, blankets and essential supplies ahead of winter. It will help fund approved recovery projects, including rebuilding homes and schools, when they go to Nepal in January. They also are looking for volunteers to join them, Lina said.

“Our plan is to go to Nepal sometimes in January to oversee the effort and do a volunteer trip,” Lina said. “We're going to invite whoever would like to come to help us do volunteer there. That way, 100 percent of the funds that are collected goes directly towards the efforts of rebuilding the lives of the families that have lost their members.”

Lina said ACF also reached out to many of the organizations across the country, such as Hindu temples and Leuva Patidar Samaj of USA. They now are collaborating with ACF.

Second mission of mercy

All four women also gathered donations for the construction of a new school in a village hit by a 2015 earthquake that also devastated Nepal. They travelled four times to oversee the project between 2015 and 2018.

“Luckily that school, which is located in this district where the flood happened, it was untouched and it's safe because it was at a much higher ground,” Patel said.

However, the flood completely wiped out a 7-story hotel where Lina and her groups would stay. Moreover, eight members of her team were killed.

“These are experienced climbers, the Sherpas,” Lina said. “There was no time for them to even go above ground.”

In 2025, members of AAHOA gathered aid for victims of the Los Angeles wildfires.

Individuals and organizations interested in supporting the ACF Nepal Relief & Recovery Fund can contribute at https://donorbox.org/acf-nepal-relief-recovery-fund.
